content: Contractures are a frequent complication associated with both neurological and non-neurological conditions. They are characterized by a reduction in joint mobility. Stretching is commonly employed as a therapeutic and preventive intervention for contractures. However, the efficacy of stretching in this context remains unclear. This review updates the original 2010 version and aims to evaluate the effects of stretching on contractures in individuals who either have or are at risk of developing them. The primary outcomes assessed include joint mobility, quality of life, pain, activity limitations, participation restrictions, spasticity, and adverse events. A comprehensive search was conducted in November 2015 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, DARE, HTA, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SCI-EXPANDED, PEDro, and trial registries. The review included randomized controlled trials and controlled clinical trials that investigated stretching as a treatment or preventive measure for contractures. Two independent reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Outcomes were evaluated in both the short term (up to one week after the last stretch) and the long term (beyond one week). The effects were expressed as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 49 studies involving 2,135 participants met the inclusion criteria. None of the studies applied stretching for more than seven months. Approximately 51% of the studies were at low risk of selection bias, but all studies were at risk of detection bias for self-reported outcomes such as pain and at risk of performance bias due to the challenges of blinding the intervention. However, most studies demonstrated low risk of detection bias for objective outcomes like range of motion, and the majority were free from attrition and selective reporting biases. These biases were unlikely to significantly influence the results, as the treatment showed minimal benefit. High-quality evidence indicated that stretching did not produce clinically meaningful short-term improvements in joint mobility for individuals with neurological conditions (MD 2°; 95% CI 0° to 3°; 26 studies, 699 participants) or non-neurological conditions (SMD 0.2; 95% CI 0 to 0.3; 19 studies, 925 participants). For individuals with neurological conditions, the short-term effects of stretching on pain (SMD 0.2; 95% CI -0.1 to 0.5; 5 studies, 174 participants) and activity limitations (SMD 0.2; 95% CI -0.1 to 0.5; 8 studies, 247 participants) were uncertain. No studies evaluated the short-term effects of stretching on quality of life or participation restrictions in this population. Adverse events were reported in five studies involving 145 participants, including skin breakdown, bruising, blisters, and pain, but statistical analysis of these data was not feasible. For individuals with non-neurological conditions, high-quality evidence demonstrated that stretching did not have clinically significant short-term effects on pain (SMD -0.2; 95% CI -0.4 to 0.1; 7 studies, 422 participants). Moderate-quality evidence suggested that stretching did not have clinically significant short-term effects on quality of life (SMD 0.3; 95% CI -0.1 to 0.7; 2 studies, 97 participants). The short-term effects of stretching on activity limitations (SMD 0.1; 95% CI -0.2 to 0.3; 5 studies, 356 participants) and participation restrictions (SMD -0.2; 95% CI -0.6 to 0.1; 2 studies, 192 participants) were uncertain. Adverse events were reported in nine studies involving 635 participants, including numbness, pain, Raynaud’s phenomenon, venous thrombosis, the need for manipulation under anesthesia, wound infections, hematoma, flexion deficits, and swelling. Statistical analysis of these adverse events was not possible. In conclusion, high-quality evidence suggests that stretching does not have clinically meaningful effects on joint mobility in individuals with or without neurological conditions when performed for less than seven months. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, even in studies with potential selection and detection biases. Subgroup analyses indicated that the effects of stretching were consistent across different types of neurological and non-neurological conditions. The effects of stretching performed for durations longer than seven months remain unexplored. Moderateand high-quality evidence suggests that stretching does not have clinically significant short-term effects on quality of life or pain in individuals with non-neurological conditions. However, the short-term effects of stretching on quality of life and pain in individuals with neurological conditions, as well as its effects on activity limitations and participation restrictions in both populations, remain uncertain.
